summary: Describes how PIM can use a Join Attribute, from RFC 5384, to build multicast trees across an MPLS network even when the network's IGP has no route to the source. This is done with a Reverse Path Forwarding vector.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a router does not know the way to where a video stream starts. This note gives it a list of stops to follow, so it can still join the stream.

questions: what is the rpf vector tlv
how does pim work across an mpls core
what is a pim join attribute
why do core routers need an rpf vector
what is a bgp free core
subtitle: How a PIM Join can carry a next-exit-router address so multicast trees can be built through a core with no external routes.

tldr.problem: Core routers in an MPLS network often have no routes to sources outside the network, so they cannot forward a PIM Join toward the root of a multicast tree.
tldr.mechanism: The edge router adds an RPF Vector, the address of the next edge router on the path to the tree root, to the PIM Join as a Join Attribute. Core routers run their RPF check on the Vector instead of on the source.
tldr.outcome: Core routers can take full part in PIM without carrying external routes. The Vector cannot ride in BSR bootstrap messages, and its security is only that of the PIM Join itself.

today: RFC 5496 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Join Attribute format in RFC 5384.

sections.title: The Problem With a Route-Free Core
sections.content:
A network can be split into edge routers, which attach to users or other networks, and core routers, which attach only to other routers of the same network. With MPLS, unicast packets headed outside the network are tunneled from one edge router to another, so core routers only need routes to the edge and core routers. One example is a BGP-free core, where the edge routers are EBGP speakers and share BGP routes only with each other.

Multicast makes this harder. With PIM-SM, PIM-SSM or BIDIR-PIM, the RFC wants core routers to be full PIM participants. That means they must send Join messages toward the root of the tree. If the root is outside the network and the core has no external routes, the Join cannot be processed and the tree cannot be built.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers in the middle of the network only know the roads inside their own town. When asked to find something far away, they have no idea which way to go.

sections.title: The RPF Vector Idea
sections.content:
The fix is a PIM extension. When an edge router sends a PIM Join into the core, it MUST include a Vector: the IP address of the next edge router along the path to the root of the distribution tree. Core routers then send the Join toward that edge router instead. The Vector acts as an attribute, within one network, for the root of the tree.

The RFC defines a new TLV for the PIM Join Attribute message from RFC 5384. It carries a single Vector that identifies the exit point of the network. Tree building is receiver driven: each router creates forwarding state and passes the Join hop by hop toward the root.

The attribute is not limited to source trees. For a shared tree, the RPF Vector TLV holds the address of a Rendezvous Point (RP), and the procedures for (S,G) Joins apply equally to (*,G) and (*,*,RP) Joins unless noted otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending the request, the router writes the address of the big edge depot on it. Every router in the middle just follows that note.

sections.title: Inserting and Processing a Vector
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, Edge 2 looks up the route to the source S and finds a BGP route whose next hop is Edge 1. It then looks up the route to Edge 1 to find its own next hop, Core 2. Edge 2 sends the Join to Core 2 with a Vector holding the address of Edge 1. Core 2 and later core routers do their RPF check on that address rather than on S.

On receipt, a router MUST first check whether the Vector address is one of its own. If so, it discards the Vector and does not pass it upstream. Otherwise it uses the Vector to find the route and passes it along in the Join it sends upstream. A router that receives a Vector MUST use it, even if it happens to have a route to the source. A router that discards a Vector MAY insert a new one, which is typical when a Join crosses a sequence of edge routers separated by route-free cores. Without periodic refreshment, Vectors expire along with the corresponding (S,G) state.

How an edge router decides whether a Vector is needed, meaning whether the core has a route to the source, is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The router at the end of the trip throws the note away because it has arrived. Everyone before it follows the note, even if they think they know a shortcut.

sections.title: Asserts, Join Suppression and Bootstrap
sections.content:
When a Join is sent toward a Vector, the PIM Assert message MUST carry the metric to the Vector rather than to the source. The Assert itself has no attribute field and does not mention the Vector. A Vector MUST NOT be sent in a Join to an upstream neighbor chosen by Assert processing if that neighbor differs from the original upstream neighbor, because only the router advertising the Vector in its IGP is guaranteed to reach it. In all other cases the Vector MUST be included.

On a LAN, downstream routers MAY include different Vectors, so an upstream router could see different Vectors over time depending on whose Join was suppressed. To keep this predictable, the Vector MUST be an extra condition in Join suppression: suppression applies only if the Vector in the Join matches the one in the multicast state. Join suppression may also be disabled on that LAN.

There is no way to carry an RPF Vector in a Bootstrap Router (BSR) bootstrap message, so the document defines no way to forward BSR messages across a core where the BSR address is not routable.
sections.plainLanguage: When several routers share a street and might send the same request, they only skip theirs if the note on it matches. That way nobody gets confused about which way to go.

sections.title: The Vector Attribute TLV
sections.content: The TLV starts with two flag bits, then a type and a length, followed by the value. The F bit (Forward Unknown TLV) means the TLV is forwarded even if the router does not understand the Type; if the type is known, the bit is ignored. The S bit (Bottom of Stack) marks the last TLV in the stack. The Vector Attribute type is 0. The value is an Encoded-Unicast address, and the length depends on its address family.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small labeled box. The label says what is inside, and inside is the address of the next stop.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The security of the RPF Vector attribute is only as strong as the security of the PIM packet carrying it, so the security considerations for PIM Join packets in RFC 4601 apply. IANA has assigned the value 0 to the RPF Vector in the PIM Join Attribute Types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is only as trustworthy as the envelope it travels in. If the envelope is safe, so is the note.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Forward Unknown TLV: forward even if the Type is not understood.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Bottom of Stack: this is the last TLV in the stack.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Depends on the address family of the Encoded-Unicast address.

fields.name: Value (Encoded-Unicast address)
fields.desc: The address of the next edge router; the field continues as needed.
